entry.content:
Advertising

Taco Bell Claims Christmas Bells Have Been Part of Its Advertising All Along

'Coca-Cola has Santa Claus. We have this'

by Shahnaz Mahmud
November 24, 2026
2:30 pm
3 min read
Share:

The cultural significance of Christmas bells in Spain is far-reaching—but do average consumers know their true symbolism? This year, Taco Bell stakes its claim via a playful conspiracy theory: “What if every Christmas bell, including Spain’s iconic New Year’s Eve chimes, has secretly been a Taco Bell advertisement all along?”

Fuego Camina Conmigo handled the work for the brand’s latest campaign, “Yes, it was us.”  The creative grew out of a different holiday. New Year’s Eve sees millions of Spaniards eat 12 grapes timed to the bell chimes that ring at midnight. But, since the fast feeder’s logo is a bell…

“Christmas is probably the biggest advertising holiday and, for some reason, it’s full of bells,” says the agency’s creative director Alvaro Florez. “They’re in the songs, in the streets, on Christmas trees. Why bells? I mean, we get the gifts and the snow, but bells? And then there’s a brand called Taco Bell. It was either a massive coincidence or the greatest marketing strategy of all time.”

“Ultimately, we wanted people to see a bell during Christmas and think of Taco Bell,” he adds. Oh, and the ad play introduces the Quesarito Deluxe.

The idea of a conspiracy theory was a perfect fit and gives consumers “something to play with rather than listen to,” Florez says. 

“The funny thing about conspiracy theories is that once you decide something is true, everything starts looking like evidence. In this case, the deeper we went, the more bells we found. At some point, it became harder to prove that Christmas wasn’t a Taco Bell campaign.”

The work brings back Josh Saunders, aka “Magikarp Guy” who became an internet sensation a decade ago on the heels of his meme that showed him in the audience during a promo for Australia’s Got Talent. It was his exaggerated expression of surprise, wide-eyed look and a dramatically open mouth that captured the world—and now Taco Bell.

“We didn’t need someone who could sell a burrito,” says Florez. “We needed someone who could capture what happens in your head when you discover something incredible that’s been right in front of your eyes all along.”

Florez underscores that casting a meme instead of a celebrity in this case was critical. Here, Saunders is widely known for one specific facial expression—which is the one Taco Bell needed to communicate the joke. He adds that using a non-celebrity feels more personal, along the lines of an inside joke, which tonally hits the right beat. 

Over the coming weeks, other films and content featuring Saunders will be released via “increasingly elaborate conspiracy theories.”

The campaign runs mainly on Instagram, Tik Tok and digital OOH.

“Coca-Cola has Santa Claus,” says Florez. “We have this. We’re not saying Taco Bell invented Christmas. We’re just saying nobody has proved otherwise.”

entry.title: For Verizon, Jonathan Bailey’s Hottie Scrooge Temps Ego Nwodim
entry.summary: Advertising For Verizon, Jonathan Bailey's Hottie Scrooge Temps Ego Nwodim She doesn't stand a ghost of a chance by David Gianatasio November 23, 2026 9:00 am 3 min read Share: Bae humbug! Ego Nwodim’s amorous ghost longs to unwrap Jonathan Bailey’s hunky Scrooge on Christmas mor
entry.content:
Advertising

For Verizon, Jonathan Bailey's Hottie Scrooge Temps Ego Nwodim

She doesn't stand a ghost of a chance

by David Gianatasio
November 23, 2026
9:00 am
3 min read
Share:

Bae humbug! Ego Nwodim’s amorous ghost longs to unwrap Jonathan Bailey’s hunky Scrooge on Christmas morning in the Verizon spot below.

“They didn’t tell me you were the sexiest man alive.”

“I’m not anymore.”

“Who said that?”

“The people.”

Celeb culture, heh.

Yes, it’s another Christmas Carol spoof. But The leads make a good team, amiably riffing on Dickens and hyping Black Friday deals with a wink and a nod. Verizon’s in-house creative team and Partizan director Amber Schaefer keep things simple, and the script makes the most of its stars’ comedic chemistry.

Here’s the requisite BTS clip:

Ricardo Aspiazu, Verizon SVP of creative & brand design, took Muse through the development process:

There are lots of Scrooges and ghosts in Xmas ads this year. Why will your version stand out?

Because nobody needed another predictable Christmas Carol. When you picture Ebenezer Scrooge, you picture a hunched-over old miser, you definitely don’t picture Jonathan Bailey looking absurdly charming. That casting choice changes the entire math of the story. Instead of playing it straight, we leaned into a cheeky, campy parody that pokes fun at every holiday ad people see every December. If you’re going to borrow a tale everyone already knows by heart, you have to flip the rules on it, keep it moving, and make people laugh.

Why do these two actors vibe for the brand?

Audiences love Jonathan from Bridgerton and Wicked, so putting him in a Victorian nightshirt as a dramatically grumpy but very handsome Scrooge gives people an instant reason to stop scrolling. Then you put Ego opposite him as the Ghost of Holiday Present. Coming off Saturday Night Live, Ego has razor-sharp timing and deadpan reactions that ground the whole bit. She doesn’t just play along with the absurdity, she heightens it.

The goal isn’t to interrupt people’s feeds. It’s to give them something worth watching. Putting a leading man and an SNL standout in a room together gave us a dynamic you wouldn’t see anywhere else.

Ego and Jonathan seem to be having a great time.

Honestly, the hardest part on set was keeping a straight face long enough to get a clean take. Watching Jonathan and Ego bounce off each other in real time was a blast. Neither of them takes themselves too seriously, and they kept pushing every line further. We ended up with so many good outtakes that we had to release them.

Credit also goes straight to our Verizon in-house creative team. Pulling off comedy at this pace while holding a high bar on film craft takes a special crew, and they delivered from the first script read to the final cut. You can tell how much fun everyone had making it.

Who’s the target audience?

During the holidays, everyone is in full shopping mode. Whether they’re buying gifts for family or quietly upgrading their own tech. Rather than slicing the audience into buckets, we wanted a story with broad, cross-generational appeal.

When they see the work, what’s the brand takeaway?

First, we want people to laugh. In many cases, Holiday advertising gets sentimental this time of year, and while there’s a place for that, we saw an open lane to lead with humor instead. Second, the deals are so good that even the most famous holiday hater can’t resist them. If you walk away smiling and Verizon is top of mind when you go to upgrade your phone or find holiday gifts, we did our job.

entry.title: The Christmas Play’s the Thing as Meta Hypes Its Smart Specs
entry.summary: Advertising The Christmas Play's the Thing as Meta Hypes Its Smart Specs 'Because the best present is being present' by David Gianatasio November 20, 2026 9:00 am 4 min read Share: Congratulations, Alice Skok ! You landed a big role in Meta’s second major holiday campaign of the
entry.content:
Advertising

The Christmas Play's the Thing as Meta Hypes Its Smart Specs

'Because the best present is being present'

by David Gianatasio
November 20, 2026
9:00 am
4 min read
Share:

Congratulations, Alice Skok! You landed a big role in Meta’s second major holiday campaign of the season. You’ll rock their AI glasses and sit in an auditorium—just sit—conveying emotion and brand attributes through gestures, attitudes and facial expressions. Everyone around you will make a godawful commotion guaranteed to lure eyeballs away from your performance. No pressure!

Alice nails it in a :60 from Mother L.A. and Prettybird director Tom Noakes. The work shows the wearable helping a mom and daughter build a deeper connection as an Xmas pageant unfolds.

“The brief was simple: Make a hall full of parents feel completely real, then make one of them stand out by doing nothing,” agency creative directors Fabio Montero and Luke Dawson tell Muse. “We shot in a real elementary school in Los Angeles, with around 100 extras holding phones in front of their faces while kids ran amok on stage.”

In recent months, Meta’s gained a dominant position among smart glasses purveyors. But the market’s cooled of late, and the tech itself remains controversial owing to privacy concerns.

Against that backdrop, “The Play” seeks to leverage EOY gifting and tout specs-driven life hacks to enhance the products’ appeal. It’s a sensible, Apple-esque approach, in line with other yuletide fare from Big Tech. The vid’s quirky and relatable, a neat combo for any brand to unwrap, especially during the yuletide.

Here, Montero and Dawson explain the strategy behind the spot.

What was the inspo? Something from real life?

Very much real life. Anyone who’s sat through a school play knows the view: a sea of raised phones and hardly a face in sight. We wondered what that looks like from the stage. An 8-year-old scanning the crowd for her mom, and for anyone who’s actually watching. It felt true, a bit funny and quietly heartbreaking, which is where the best Christmas stories live. Nobody had phones at my school plays, but I see it everywhere now among parents of our generation.

What’s the big brand takeaway?

That the best technology gets out of the way. Meta Glasses let you capture the moment, take a call or ask a question without reaching for your phone, so you stay in the room. We want people to feel a lump in the throat, then a grin, then a quiet thought about where their own phone is. Because the best present is being present.

Put us on set. What went down during the shoot?

The costumes were half the fun. They had to look homemade, a little wonky and full of love, like every parent’s best effort the night before. Our young lead, Harlow O’Connor, had to scan row after row of phones in the silent moment before she finds her mom. She was incredible, and a little petrified by the sheer number of extras in front of her, so the nerves you see on screen are almost the real thing.

Harlow does a nice job, it’s a very natural performance.

Luckily, Harlow has a twin sister, Rowan, just as talented, so we could swap them between shots. Choreographing 100 extras and 20 odd eight year olds in costumes is a lot, even for a director who’s a child at heart, like Tom Noakes.

So many holiday ads though, especially for tech. Why will this stand out?

Every other Christmas ad asks you to look at the screen. Ours asks you to look up. Meta is a tech brand whose hero film is about putting the tech down, and the glasses are the only thing in the room not pulling anyone’s attention. Charming, not cheesy, and no snow globe in sight.

entry.content:

He'll Be Back ... for Christmas. Arnold Schwarzenegger x Amazon Score Week's Best Campaign

Apple, McDonald's, Meta and Vital Cannabis round out our Top 5

by David Gianatasio
November 19, 2026
9:45 am
2 min read
Share:

Here’s our run-down of the week’s top work, chosen by the Clios staff.

Best: Arnold Schwarzenegger Pumps Up Xmas in a Santa Suit for Amazon

Arnie muscles his way through a holiday romp as Kris Kringle, sampling the season’s simple pleasures in NYC. “Lifting’s kind of my thing,” he quips in one sequence, tossing a pine tree javelin-style onto the top of a car. From Hungryman director Wayne McClammy and Amazon’s in-house team. Read More

2. McDonald’s Brings Macaulay Culkin Home for the Holidays

He’s a few miles from home, actually. But definitely still alone. Like Ahhhnold above, this marks another triumph of nostalgic celeb casting. M.C. cuts up as Kevin McCallister in a Mickey D’s on a snowy night after closing time. From Wieden+Kennedy Toronto and directors Ramy Youssef and Amir Farhang. Read More

3. For the Holidays, Apple Helps Make an Artist’s Dream Come True

TBWA\MAL and director Melina Matsoukas present a memorable tear-jerker about a young artist who gets a very special gift. (It’s a Mac. D’uh.) Paintings and sculptures by Hebru Brantley add a bright, bold dimension. Read More

4. Meta Dramatically Reframes the Holidays and Its AI Glasses in ‘Window Shopping’

There’s gorgeous craft on display from Mother L.A. and director Max Siedentopf of Division. It’s old-timey but high-tech too, celebrating the joys of brick-and-mortar shopping in our age of digital wonders and online overload. Read More

5. ‘Nug on the Rug’ Spreads Cheer. So Be Nice, Not Naughty

Heads up, it’s the holidays. (Heh.) Bandits & Friends rolls the perfect tone for Vivid Cannabis, with a budding Xmas character guaranteed to go up in smoke. Read More

entry.title: Grey U.S. CCO Samira Ansari on Bringing Out the Best in Her Team to Get the Best Results for Clients
entry.summary: Advertising Grey U.S. CCO Samira Ansari on Bringing Out the Best in Her Team to Get the Best Results for Clients 'I tell creatives to go rogue, and I will have their back ' by Lalita Salgaokar November 19, 2026 8:00 am 6 min read Share: Samira Ansari Samira Ansari is a powerhouse
entry.content:
Advertising

Grey U.S. CCO Samira Ansari on Bringing Out the Best in Her Team to Get the Best Results for Clients

'I tell creatives to go rogue, and I will have their back '

by Lalita Salgaokar
November 19, 2026
8:00 am
6 min read
Share:
Samira Ansari

Samira Ansari is a powerhouse. I first sat down with her 10 years ago while she was at Grey as a creative director. It’s been super inspiring following her career over the years. Now, she’s back at Grey as chief creative officer. We met once again in her office to talk about creativity and what’s continuing to keep her excited about the work, the people and the clients’ business 10 years later.

It’s hard to sum up on the highlights of a full decade, but could you tell us your top 3 since 2016?

A lot has happened. I had a baby. Not a highlight, but Covid happened. And it changed our life. It changed everything. I did some really good work for Michelob Ultra. And then we did “McEnroe vs. McEnroe.” And then I became a CCO for the first time. It’s been a great big experience. So, I kind of grew into myself a little bit—I grew up.

Your work continues to have a strong sense of humor. Does that continue to be intentional?

We’re in the entertainment business. Apparently, people spend five hours a day with creators. We’re competing with entertainment. And being funny is one of the ways you entertain. Don’t we all need a laugh right now, with everything that’s happening? If we can do that, why wouldn’t we? There’s a time and place for comedy, but I’ve always loved it.

You’ve helped BIG agencies win BIG awards. What are the few things you start getting into when you get a new position?

It’s not me. It’s the people that do all the work. You just put the right people with the right brands and magic can happen. I tell creatives to go rogue, and I will have their back. That’s my job as a CCO: to bring the best out of people and to get the best for our clients. I recently created a presentation on what I learned about being a CCO from my toddler. In both jobs, you learn that you’re managing sensitive people. So, it isn’t me, really. I can’t do this alone. I have so many people backing me up and supporting me along the way.

Any advice on client relationship building for creatives?

If we don’t feel and understand the client’s business, we’re bad marketers. If we don’t know what climate their business is operating in, if we don’t know their business problems, even before they do, then we can’t be good marketing partners. When I started 25 years ago, the creatives were kept in the back of the office. Now, we have a seat at the table because we can be business partners. And I have a completely different relationship with our clients than our CEO or head of strategy does. We all play different parts. But we’re all part of the client’s business.

How do you balance fighting for your team while being a business partner to clients?

Ultimately, I’m responsible for the creative outcome of the agency. What we put out in the world is what keeps me up at night, it’s a big responsibility. I do have to keep an eye on everything. But I can’t do it all by myself. It’s a balance of making sure the right talent is on the right pieces of business—and then pushing everything forward, keeping an eye on everything and picking your battles.

How are you filling your creative cup?

I’m watching a lot of kids’ shows right now. I make sure that I’ve seen at least one or two episodes of every interesting show that’s happening. I do spend a lot of time on TikTok. TikTok fascinates me because it is addictive for all the reasons it’s successful. I’m fascinated with just how entertaining the average person is. As a marketer, you have to be aware of all that stuff.

Where do brands and ad spend go in the creator economy?

When brands throw money at creators without building a presence or personality, in the long game, they lose because then they must keep throwing money at creators. But when I see content from a brand I know, and a brand that I love and respect, it sticks in my brain, because the brand-building work has been done. You need people to love your brand before buying your products. So, it’s a balance of both things.

I’m curious about your opinion on coaching for creatives. How beneficial is it?

I got my first CCO gig at Deutsch New York, and they were amazing. I did a lot of learning there and I came to Ogilvy with that background. Many CCOs that I didn’t even know reached out to me very kindly and said, “Congrats and if I were you, I’d ask for a coach.” I was never really a believer in a coach.

Then, when I met my coach, he was amazing. We didn’t even talk about work or how I showed up. He said, “In 10 years’ time when you look back, how do you want to remember your time at this organization? As a moment in your life, where do you want this to be?” And I think that changed my approach. My coaches have always helped me and it’s a safe space to get things off your chest. Coaches have helped me with putting boundaries on myself, managing my time and not being apologetic about it.

What’s your advice on negotiating your worth as a creative?

When you work hard and you deliver results, I think you do get compensated for it. And if you’re not being compensated for it, then maybe you’re not in the right place. But you should always ask for what you think you want and then negotiate. But I do know that someone once said to me, “Know your worth, ask for what you want, take the calls. Do lunch once a month.” My coach told me that. He’s like, “Always reach out to people that are good for your network. Meet people. Take the phone calls even if that’s a job you don’t want.” It is worth it, because it’s networking. Show up for yourself as a brand. The first piece of advice someone gave me at 23 was to build your own brand. You have to treat yourself as a brand and then that brand develops worth.

entry.title: Meta Dramatically Reframes the Holidays and Its AI Glasses in ‘Window Shopping’
entry.summary: Advertising Meta Dramatically Reframes the Holidays and Its AI Glasses in 'Window Shopping' Handcrafted designs help tell the tale by David Gianatasio November 17, 2026 9:00 am 3 min read Share: Meta’s all about the Christmas decorations in “Window Shopping,” an eye-pleasing effo
entry.content:
Advertising

Meta Dramatically Reframes the Holidays and Its AI Glasses in 'Window Shopping'

Handcrafted designs help tell the tale

by David Gianatasio
November 17, 2026
9:00 am
3 min read
Share:

Meta’s all about the Christmas decorations in “Window Shopping,” an eye-pleasing effort from Mother L.A. The campaign presents ornate retail window displays, decked out for the season, to entice viewers into the company’s Meta Lab stores.

Max Siedentopf of Division directed a half-dozen quick spots, showing off Ray-Ban Meta glasses and other wares to fine effect.

“Meta Lab is set up for you to experience wearables through interesting demos, settings and events,” agency creative director Tobias Linborg tells Muse. “We wanted to intrigue people to visit by giving them a peek inside without telling the full story. The holiday windows allowed us to do just that.”

“Each window was conceptualized around the products you can find in the store, while leaning into Holiday tropes and semiotics like advent calendars, snow globes and workshops,” Linborg says.

“Once we shared our designs with Max Siedentopf, he and our production designer, Andy Hillman, elevated them further. Our production team then built these windows for real.”

“It was important for us to do that. Not just to have the extra charm and handmade feel around the work, but also to help convey that Meta Lab is a real place you can go to. If you make everything look too digital, that becomes less clear.”

It feels like every brand’s stressing IRL authenticity and handcrafted products this yuletide season. For tech titans, slinging AI, that can seem like a bit of a stretch. But Apple pulls it off by positioning its laptops as creative helpers and tapping an acclaimed artist to make paintings the old fashioned way. Though not strictly speaking an Xmas effort, Shopify’s global push—also from Mother—compellingly hypes the platform’s prowess for helping humans build small businesses.

Meta’s approach plays equally well. There are brick-and-mortar stores to visit, so the snazzy windows work in context, providing comfortable, nostalgic framing devices for high-tech gadgetry.

“We wanted each window to have an element of magic, to create a display only Meta could do,” Linborg says. “That’s where things like the VR lasers, the UFO beam or the floating Meta Glasses tree came to be.”

This BTS clip breaks it down:

To their credit, the spots do just enough to beguile, avoiding narrative overkill.

“Christmas ads tend to let the viewer sit back and enjoy a complete story,” he says. “These are quick vignettes that do the opposite. They are designed to make you curious about Meta Lab, without fully explaining the store or revealing [everything] you can find inside.”

“To complete the story, you have to go and visit for yourself.”

entry.title: Tyler Newman of Unfold on Marketers Running Up That Hill
entry.summary: 2 Minutes With Tyler Newman of Unfold on Marketers Running Up That Hill 'If we're not challenging the expected, we're not pushing creativity far enough' by Shahnaz Mahmud November 16, 2026 9:00 am Share: Tyler Newman | Photo illustration by Gautami Upadhyay “The wave of creators
entry.content:
2 Minutes With

Tyler Newman of Unfold on Marketers Running Up That Hill

'If we're not challenging the expected, we're not pushing creativity far enough'

by Shahnaz Mahmud
November 16, 2026
9:00 am
Share:
Tyler Newman | Photo illustration by Gautami Upadhyay

“The wave of creators making hugely successful feature films, like Curry Barker’s Obsession and Kane Parsons’ Backrooms, is shaping culture and our industry,” says Unfold’s Tyler Newman. “Nobody’s leaning into this as impressively as Blumhouse, who I get to collaborate with closely on the brand marketing side. There’s a lot Hollywood can learn from this approach.”

Tyler serves as VP of social and integrated marketing at the Los Angeles-based independent creative and integrated marketing agency that specializes in digital campaigns, social media and events for entertainment, gaming, sports and consumer brands. 

An Emmy-winning documentary producer, his credits include HBO’s Natalie Wood: What Remains Behind, which premiered at the Sundance Film Festival.

We spent a few minutes with Tyler to learn about his background, inspirations and on always maintaining a sense of play.

What creative hill would you die on?

Coming from an agency perspective, our job is to constantly push boundaries. So, we should always have a creative hill to climb. If we’re not challenging the expected, we’re not pushing creativity far enough.

What meme or GIF sums up your creative process?

The Charlie Day Conspiracy Board. In entertainment marketing, especially social, we absorb such a high volume of information—whether from creative briefs, comment sections, trends or the news. There’s no avoiding this influx. So, keeping the chaos organized is key. And often, finding connections between seemingly disparate data points results in the best content. Even if sometimes we look crazy doing so.

What source of inspiration do you return to constantly?

There’s a quote from Mad Men that I often come back to. Don is giving advice. He says, “Peggy, just think about it. Deeply. Then forget it. And an idea will jump up in your face.” I have two dogs, so I usually walk at least two hours per day. It’s during those times that I often have my biggest breakthroughs and solve problems that I had been struggling through. 

What newsletter, creator or account should everyone follow?

The podcast Opening Weekend: Selling Hollywood with Jim Fredrick. Shoutout to my Chapman professor, Jim Fredrick, who inspired me to pursue entertainment marketing. (And he won the Clios Impact award last year)!

What’s the last great book, article or video you consumed?

I’m a big Lance Oppenheim fan, and with his films Primetime and You Can See Everything having moments, I’d urge everyone to watch his 10-minute New York Times documentary, “The Happiest Guy in the World.” It’s a masterclass in short-form, introspective storytelling. 

What’s your main strength as a creative person?

Always maintaining a sense of play—trying new things and expanding your imagination, but also employing a bit of game theory to the creative process. For example, understanding fan motivations, using data to anticipate behavior and knowing when to change the rules are all part of a process centered around play. 

Tell us about a recent project you’re proud of.

Our work on DC Studios’ Lanterns for HBO Max. Early in the anticipation phase of our campaign, we realized our social approach wasn’t resonating the way we’d hoped. We adjusted our content and community engagement strategy to ensure core fans felt heard. Lanterns ultimately became DC Studios’ biggest series premiere on the platform and consistently trended No. 1 on X. I’m particularly proud of how our team responded and grateful to the flexibility of our partners at HBO. It’s a reminder that great social is about both your initial strategy as a willingness to pivot and listen to your audience. 

Another project I’m incredibly proud of is our recently launched “Pass It On” campaign for Rakuten Viki, starring K-pop sensation LE SSERAFIM. We’re always looking for ways to connect brands with culture in ways that feel authentic. And this campaign brought together two passionate audiences: K-pop and K-drama fans. We handled creative development through execution. It was a great example of what can happen when strong creative, the right talent, and genuine fandom come together.

What would you be doing if you weren’t in advertising?

I loved being a camp counselor growing up, so I’d go back to that!  

You’ve got 2 minutes with the industry. What’s your hot take?

Rather than chasing the latest trends, brands can create more lasting value by investing in original content series. And when it comes to measuring social performance, follower count is just one piece of the pie. I like shares, sentiment and non-follower reach.

2 Minutes With is our regular interview series where we chat with creatives about their backgrounds, creative inspirations, work they admire and more. For more about 2 Minutes With, or to be considered for the series, please get in touch.

entry.title: Shopify Says Even a Pimple Can Spark Big Ideas for Entrepreneurs
entry.summary: Advertising Shopify Says Even a Pimple Can Spark Big Ideas for Entrepreneurs Hyping the platform's power to help build new businesses by David Gianatasio November 13, 2026 9:00 am 5 min read Share: Whoa! That zit gives me a great idea… Shopify spotlights four diverse, quirky entr
entry.content:
Advertising

Shopify Says Even a Pimple Can Spark Big Ideas for Entrepreneurs

Hyping the platform's power to help build new businesses

by David Gianatasio
November 13, 2026
9:00 am
5 min read
Share:

Whoa! That zit gives me a great idea…

Shopify spotlights four diverse, quirky entrepreneurial ventures in its first work from Mother L.A. Lensed in bouncy, pseudo-doc style by Iconoclast director Marcus Ibanez, “Just an Idea” hypes the platform’s Sidekick AI commerce assistant and follows four very different startups.

There’s an offbeat but earnest tone throughout, with the most memorable bits involving high schoolers who develop pimple patches. That one really … pops. (Well, it does!) The other segments involve apparel, a sofa for dogs and a decal that stops pigeons from crashing into windows, and the brisk pace propels viewers effortlessly through the spot’s 2-minute run-time.

“Anyone who’s ever wanted to build something of their own just got powerful enough to do it,” Neal Hicks, director of creative at Shopify, tells Muse.

“For years, a lot of people with great ideas talked themselves out of them: ‘I don’t have the money. I don’t have the time. I don’t have the experience. I didn’t go to the right school.’ Those reasons were real. But with AI, if you’ve got an idea and the courage and determination to go for it, you can give it a shot and make it real.”

At its core, the work is about technology powering self-expression and turning visions into reality. In that sense, it shares themes with Apple’s 2026 holiday spot, in which a MacBook Neon helps a young painter strive for his goals. Shopify focuses on business, but the underlying message is the same: AI’s one more tool in your kit. It shouldn’t be feared, but harnessed by humans seeking to unlock their true potential. AI is transformational—in many instances, it can help us grow and change for the better.

Here, Hicks chats with Muse about campaign development.

Did you base the film on real user stories?

We meet founders every day, of every age and from all over the world. Their ideas are inspiring, joyful and sometimes wonderfully strange. For a long time there was a cliché about who an entrepreneur was and what they looked like. That’s completely broken down now, and we wanted the film to reflect that.

The startup types are a tad offbeat, no?

We started with a skeleton of the kinds of people and ideas we see every day, and the reasons each of them might have thought, “I could never actually do that. It’s not for people like me.” The real unlock came when Marcus took those sketches and turned them into people you want to root for. A guy with a sketchbook and great taste. An office worker tired of birds hitting his window. A couple fed up with ugly dog beds. A group of high school seniors with an idea for pimple patches. Marcus deserves a lot of credit for that.

Is the viewer takeaway as simple as: Shopify’s there for you?

“Just An Idea” is for people who haven’t started a business yet, including many who’ve never thought of themselves as entrepreneurs or even really considered it. But honestly, what we care about most is how people feel about themselves when the film ends. We want them to feel a door open, like they could actually do something with the idea they’ve tucked in the back of their mind for so long. If someone watches it and thinks, “You know what? Maybe now I can,” then it worked.

Not a holiday ad per se, but it has that vibe.

That’s fair. I think the message fits this time of year. The new year is all about new beginnings, and what we’re really saying is: Why not make this the year you stop saying no to that idea you’ve always kept small, and turn it into something real? Take your shot. Because now, all you need to get started is just an idea.

You squeezed a lot into 120 seconds. Any big challenges making the film?

Honestly, it was one of the most joyful sets I’ve ever been on, and that wasn’t a given. We shot in Barcelona over six days, with four stories, a lot of locations, and all of it on film. So there was no room to overshoot.

Then, in the middle of the night before day one, our phones started going off with storm warnings. I remember sitting in video village while the rain came down so hard that water was running in under our feet. I looked up and literally watched a chair blow past. Then I looked back at the monitor, saw that shot of Milo [the fashionista in the cafe] and thought… that’s beautiful. All that chaos outside, and something so beautiful being made inside. That’s when I knew we were part of something special.

Walter [the bird guy] was a character a lot of us fell in love with. When the actor playing him wrapped his final scene, the whole crew, Marcus and our cinematographer Kasper Tuxen included, stood up and gave him an ovation. We ended up doing that for most of the cast, and I think it says a lot about the feeling on that set.

Netflix Swims Away With Ad-of-the-Week Honors

Plus: SickKids, Amazon, Xfinity, Verizon ... and the Clio Awards

by David Gianatasio
November 12, 2026
12:00 pm
2 min read
Share:

Here’s a rundown of the week’s best work, ranked by the Clios’ staff.

Bestie: Astronauts, Vampires and Adorable Amphibians Can’t Get Enough of Their Favorite Netflix Shows

Mother explores the intensity of fandom in three different settings: outer space, a vampire’s neighborhood and a fancy fish tank. All three spots absolutely slap, but the Bridgerton-besotted aquatic salamander swam (and walked!) into our hearts. From Netflix’s Brand Creative Studio and Iconoclast directors Vania Heymann and Gal Muggia. Read More and view the others here

2. Turning Donors Into Lifelines for SickKids Hospital

IV lines become symbols of life across time and space, aiding a young girl in her fight for survival. TBWA\Canada crafted this artful appeal with director Nico Perez Veiga from Iconoclast-Merchant. Powerhouse imagery helps it rank among the best health and wellness ads of the year. Read More

3. Amazon’s Christmas Epic Is About the Journey, Not So Much the Destination

The Beatles’ “Golden Slumbers” propels the retail kingpin’s short film, titled “Joy Delivered.” The track’s sleepy fairytale quality matches the snowy scenes from Amazon’s in-house team and Smuggler director Mark Molloy. Read More

4. In Xfinity’s Holiday Spot, John C. Reilly Wants You to Savor Every Moment—IRL, Not Online

The Oscar nominee plays a ghost in this Dickens riff about looking up from your damn screens and enjoying the holidays already. From Goodby Silverstein & Partners and O Positive director Jim Jenkins. Read More

5. Martin Short Elfs Himself for Verizon and We’re So There for It

Marty dominates this Santa’s Workshop spoof, chewing scenery like he’s gobbling down an Xmas ham. From the carrier’s in-house team and directors Jocelyn DeBoer and Dawn Luebbe. Read More

Special Mention: The Clio Awards Painted a Guy Gold in Its 2027 Call for Entries Campaign

We love our own work—deal with it! Srsly, this one’s good as gold. Beyond Studios exec and social-media star Cole Poska glitters in the central role. He showered after the shoot (probably). Read More

entry.title: For the Holidays, Apple Helps Make a Young Artist’s Dream Come True
entry.summary: Advertising For the Holidays, Apple Helps Make a Young Artist's Dream Come True Hebru Brantley created the artworks in a film directed by Melina Matsoukas by David Gianatasio November 12, 2026 8:45 am 3 min read Share: Some folks suffer for their art. But a MacBook Neo can give c
entry.content:
Advertising

For the Holidays, Apple Helps Make a Young Artist's Dream Come True

Hebru Brantley created the artworks in a film directed by Melina Matsoukas

by David Gianatasio
November 12, 2026
8:45 am
3 min read
Share:

Some folks suffer for their art. But a MacBook Neo can give creators the tools they need to realize their vision.

Running nearly 4 minutes, Apple’s 2026 holiday campaign tells such a story in sweet, starkly emotional terms. Developed by TBWA\Media Arts Lab, the film follows a young man’s quest for self-expression.

As a little kid and teenager, he flexes his talent by painting on his bedroom wall, skateboards and sneakers. His teachers and school friends just don’t understand—they even grow hostile at times. But his nurturing parents understand, providing support and gifts—both physical and emotional—to help him stay the course and find his way.

Strawberry Guy’s “Give Me a Dream” sets a dreamy-pop mood that fits the realism on screen from director Melina Matsoukas and cinematographer Bradford Young. Unlike many yuletide ads this year, many of which engage in flights of fancy and harness animation techniques, Apple keeps us grounded in the here and now, spinning a hopeful tale and summoning tears—but never leaning too hard on sentimentality.

Hebru Brantley created the various paintings and sculptures, adding a rich tactile language to the storyline, and the project hit close to home.

“Our experiences shape what we create. My mother saw the artist in me before I could see it in myself, and her belief gave me the confidence to explore that—which I’ll continue to honor,” he says. “That’s why this story is special to me. The right tools can help us unlock our creativity. For the young artist in the film, the MacBook Neo is also a reminder that his parents see the potential in him, and an invitation to reconnect with it.”

This BTS puts his efforts in perspective:

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Hello Apple (@helloapple)

It’s useful to consider the work in light of the stop-motion avalanche of Xmas ads this year. Those brands play up the painstaking craft behind their adverts to symbolize caring and quality in the age of AI. That’s all well and good, and such tactics probably resonate with many viewers who remain leery of generative advancements.

Here, Apple takes a somewhat different tack, tapping into raw emotions and youthful aspirations to sell laptops that put AI at our fingertips.

The tech giant trumpets its horn in a slightly different way, positioning itself as the source for innovations that can make users’ most cherished, hard-fought dreams a reality.
